newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn denies gold sale plan, Waigel heads to c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Bonn denies gold sale plan, Waigel heads to c.bank.

text.p: Germany's finance ministry denied on Wednesday that the government was planning to sell off the Bundesbank's gold, but appeared to be considering balance sheet moves to realise the central bank's assets.
Speculation is growing that a move to change the Bundesbank's accounting practices could be in the works as Bonn seeks ways to meet the budget deficit target for joining the single European currency.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel arrived in Frankfurt on Thursday morning to take part in a Bundesbank council meeting, after attending a debate on European economic and monetary union (EMU) in Bonn.
Government sources said Waigel would discuss an increase in the book value of the central bank's gold, which would boost the central bank's profit, but he was not discussing gold sales.

Germany, once the star candidate for EMU membership, is seeking desperately to rein in its budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product or less to make sure it qualifies for the euro's launch in 1999.
The issue has become yet more urgent as experts from federal, state and local governments are expected to announce a shortfall of 20 billion marks ($12 billion) in tax revenues later on Thursday.
The talk of gold sales and asset revaluation follows the announcement on Wednesday that Bonn is considering an early sale of some of its Deutsche Telekom shares.

A Finance Ministry spokeswoman said on Thursday in response to Reuter enquiries that Germany had no plans to sell gold to aid the federal budget. It also had no plans to make any such recommendation to the Bundesbank.
But both the Finance Ministry and the central bank declined to be drawn on whether a revaluation of the assets was planned.
The gold price fell in reponse although dealers said a weaker dollar had encouraged some buying which limited the losses. Bullion was fixed in the morning in London $1 lower at $347.10 an ounce.
Germany's Handelsblatt newspaper reported on Thursday that the ruling coalition was considering using the bank's reserves to avoid raising taxes this year to offset the shortfall in tax income.

Coalition sources confirmed to Reuters that plans had been drawn up in this direction. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), are particularly opposed to an increase in indirect taxation to top up budget coffers.

A second newspaper, the Berliner Zeitung, also said in an advance report for its Friday edition that Waigel was seeking a higher valuation of Bundesbank's foreign exchange and gold assets to raise further cash for the budget.
The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price, a method which is normal under German book-keeping regulations.

A revaluation could bring a huge windfall profit to the bank. In gold alone, the Bundesbank holds 95 million ounces originally acquired at an average price of 144 marks an ounce, for a total value of 13.7 billion marks.
At the current market value of about 600 marks an ounce, it would be worth about 57 billion marks.

Yet even if Bonn could succeed in freeing funds tied up in the central bank's 95 million ounces of gold, it was not immediately clear how or whether these could be used to help Germany in its efforts to meet the EMU criteria.

Sources said an outright sale of gold to realise the assets appeared unlikely, given that Germany has led a vocal campaign opposing sales of only a small proportion of the International Monetary Fund's gold assets.

A simple revaluation of the assets to closer to the market price is technically allowed under German book-keeping laws. But it would mark a change from the established practice. One source said this could even require a change in the Bundesbank law.
Even once those assets are revalued, it is unclear how the resulting extraordinary profit could be transferred to Bonn in a way which would genuinely help the deficit to be reduced.
Conventionally, Bonn uses any profit over a budgeted amount of seven billion marks to repay old debt. It need not necessarily use a special profit in this way.
But a transfer of that money to the cover the budget deficit would probably run into problems when it came to assessing which country meets the criteria.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistical agency, declined to comment on this specific case. But Eurostat's acting director Daniel Byk told Reuters that EU rules stating that a nation cannot reduce its deficit through central bank gold sales applied to all member nations.
EU rules state that gold sales from central banks can be used only to reduce the government debt, but not to cut the deficit.

A further monetary source, commenting directly on the German case, said that in his view the EU rules would not allow a government to revalue a central bank's gold reserves and book the increased value into the budget to reduce the deficit.
